claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified FeNiCrMn is controlled by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition in dislocation mobility.
Low temperatures and high strain rates kinetically constrain dislocation motion in FeNiCrMn.
Kinetically constrained dislocation motion produces high strain hardening through dislocation pile-up and limited cross-slip.
Higher temperatures and slower strain rates enhance thermally activated cross-slip and dynamic recovery.
Enhanced cross-slip and dynamic recovery reduce strain hardening.
The proposed specimens are made by arc melting and ingot metallurgy, followed by homogenization and solution treatment.
The intended initial microstructure is single-phase, uniform, and equiaxed.
Systematically changing test temperature and strain rate will promote the proposed transition in dislocation dynamics.
Dislocation density, arrangement, and cross-slip activity mediate the transition between kinetically limited glide and dynamic recovery.
Temperature and strain rate modify the activation behavior of dislocation cross-slip and motion.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation produces pronounced dislocation pile-up and planar slip.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation permits dislocation cross-slip and rearrangement, enabling dynamic recovery.
FeNiCrMn will have higher flow stress under low-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions than under high-temperature, low-strain-rate conditions.
FeNiCrMn will have higher strain-hardening rates under low-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions than under high-temperature, low-strain-rate conditions.
The alloy will retain overall ductility because of its inherent strength-ductility balance.
The hypothesis is restricted to similarly processed, single-phase, homogenized FeNiCrMn.
Secondary phases, heavy pre-deformation, or non-equilibrium processing may make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Analogous high- and medium-entropy-alloy studies support the proposed dislocation-mediated mechanism.
The transition temperatures, transition strain rates, and relative contributions of pile-up and cross-slip are not yet quantitatively known.
Failure to observe either the predicted mechanical trend or the corresponding reduction in cross-slip and recovery at low temperature and high strain rate would falsify the hypothesis.
